clue.text: Out of service, like Hanley's harbour?

definitions.meaning: a shop or road that is shut, not open for use
James Hanley wrote the novel The ... Harbour

explanation.definitionFit: Something out of service is shut, and Hanley's harbour in his novel's title is the shut one.

clue.text: Polish (or Danish) poet is a fallen angel

indicators.note: a fallen angel has tumbled from grace, so the letters of the word tumble into a new order

explanation.surface: A poet from Poland or Denmark is described as a fallen angel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fallen' rearranges ANGEL. Antoni Lange was a Polish poet and Per Lange a Danish one, hence the bracketed hedge.
explanation.definitionFit: Lange is the surname of a Polish poet (Antoni) and of a Danish poet (Per).

clue.text: Somerset Maugham's conclusion

definitions.meaning: Maugham's 1938 book of reflections is titled The ...
a final review or recap of an argument

explanation.definitionFit: A final recap of an argument is its close, and that recap phrase is also the title of Maugham's memoir.

clue.text: Ancient Greek League relating to English composer

definitions.meaning: the alliance of Greek city-states led by Athens, based on the island of Delos
an adjective formed from Frederick Delius, the English composer

explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian alliance took its name from Delos, and the same adjective can describe the music of Delius.

clue.text: Tom Sharpe's revelation is most improper

definitions.meaning: Tom Sharpe wrote the comic novel ... Exposure, a revelation being an exposure
highly offensive to decency

explanation.definitionFit: Highly offensive conduct is obscene, and Sharpe's novel pairs that adjective with exposure, here called a revelation.

clue.text: Gee, a mafioso city destroyed in Fuller work!

indicators.note: a city destroyed is broken apart, so these letters are wrecked and rebuilt in a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a Mafia-run city being razed, in a book by Fuller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'destroyed' rearranges GEEAMAFIOSOCITY. Roy Fuller's 1956 novel is the definition; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Roy Fuller, the English poet and novelist, published a novel under this title in 1956.

clue.text: Verses expected to stand on their own two feet

definitions.text: Verses expected to stand on their own two feet

parts.words: Verses expected to stand on their own two feet
parts.note: the idiom for being independent is read literally: lines of verse made of exactly two metrical feet

explanation.definitionFit: A line of verse of two metrical feet takes this name from Greek for 'two measures'.

clue.text: Dust jacket or disguise (her features) in James book

definitions.meaning: the paper wrapper round a book
P. D. James's first novel is ... Her Face, to hide a face being to conceal it

explanation.definitionFit: A dust jacket is a book's outer wrapper, and to hide her face is the verb in the title of P. D. James's debut.

clue.text: Godden bloomer would not show up well on

definitions.text: Godden bloomer would not show up well on

parts.words: Godden bloomer would not show up well on
parts.note: A black flower would not show up well on a black background, the colour word implied by the title

explanation.surface: A flower from a Rumer Godden title would vanish against its background.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue gives the novel's title minus its first word: the missing 'Black' completes both the title and the phrase 'would not show up well on black'.
explanation.definitionFit: The flower of Rumer Godden's Black Narcissus is the daffodil genus, its title naming it.

clue.text: Where some were more equal than others 4

definitions.text: Where some were more equal than others

parts.words: Where some were more equal than others
parts.note: Orwell's slogan 'all animals are equal, but some are more equal than others' is set on the farm of his fable

explanation.definitionFit: Orwell's fable sets the pigs' slogan of unequal equality on a farm run by its livestock.

clue.text: Melville's skipper, ever unreliable

indicators.note: something unreliable cannot be trusted to stay put, so the letters shift into a new order

explanation.surface: Herman Melville's sea captain is said to be always untrustworthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unreliable' rearranges EVER. Captain Vere commands HMS Bellipotent in Melville's Billy Budd.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain Vere is the commander of the warship in Melville's Billy Budd.

clue.text: Unattached, like de Montherlant's protagonists

definitions.meaning: single, unmarried and abstaining
Henry de Montherlant's novel Les Célibataires (The Bachelors) follows unmarried men

explanation.definitionFit: An unattached person is single and chaste, as are the bachelor heroes of Montherlant's novel.

clue.text: Ainsworth's knight of the road confuses tip and run

indicators.note: to confuse things is to jumble them, so the letters of the two words are jumbled together

explanation.surface: A highwayman in Ainsworth's novel mixes up a cricket phrase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confuses' rearranges TIP and RUN together. Tip and run is a form of cricket; Dick Turpin is the highwayman in Ainsworth's Rookwood.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Turpin is the highwayman hero of Harrison Ainsworth's Rookwood; a knight of the road is a highway robber.

clue.text: Austrian composer reaches height in South Africa

definitions.meaning: Alban ..., composer of Wozzeck
in Afrikaans a mountain, as in the Drakensberg

explanation.definitionFit: Alban Berg was a Viennese composer, and the Afrikaans word for a mountain shares his surname.

clue.text: Descriptive of a Gray thought in a green shade, perhaps?

definitions.text: Descriptive of a Gray thought in a green shade, perhaps?

parts.words: Descriptive of a Gray thought in a green shade, perhaps?
parts.note: Marvell's 'a green thought in a green shade' is bent to Thomas Gray, whose famous mournful poem was written in a country churchyard

explanation.surface: A colour-themed riff on a line of Marvell.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray is the poet Thomas Gray, not a colour; his Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard is a thought in the green shade of the churchyard.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes mournful verse like Gray's Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard.

clue.text: Beethoven piece for Shaw heroine?

definitions.meaning: Beethoven's piano bagatelle in A minor
German für means 'for', and the name is close to Eliza Doolittle of Shaw's Pygmalion

explanation.definitionFit: Beethoven's bagatelle is titled in German 'for Elise', a near twin of Shaw's flower girl Eliza.

clue.text: Colette's gentlewoman, hardly a gentlewoman

definitions.meaning: Colette's novel about Minne was published in English as The Gentle ...
a dissolute, licentious person, the opposite of a well-bred lady

explanation.definitionFit: A dissolute rake is no lady, yet Colette's English title calls her heroine a gentle one.

clue.text: Many cavort, not returning for authoress

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, i.e. many
to romp is to frolic or cavort

indicators.note: returning means the word not is read backwards

explanation.surface: Lots of people frolic, never going home, to stand in for a woman writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns NOT into TON. Richmal Crompton wrote the Just William books.
explanation.definitionFit: Richmal Crompton, creator of Just William, was a woman writer, the old word for which is authoress.

clue.text: Doomed vessel sheers up somehow

indicators.note: somehow says the letters arrive by some unstated route, i.e. in a rearranged order

explanation.surface: A ship destined to sink swerves upward by some means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'somehow' rearranges SHEERS and UP. Longfellow's The Wreck of the Hesperus tells of the doomed schooner.
explanation.definitionFit: Longfellow's ballad The Wreck of the Hesperus tells of a schooner lost in a storm.

clue.text: Black companion of 12

explanation.surface: A dark partner to the highwayman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black' is the first word of the horse's name, not a colour of the companion's skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Dick Turpin's legendary mare, ridden from London to York, was named Black Bess.

clue.text: Reportedly severe writer

indicators.note: reportedly means the word for severe is heard, not spelt

explanation.surface: A writer said to be harsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' says the word is heard: STERN for 'severe' sounds the same as the surname of Laurence Sterne, author of Tristram Shandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne wrote Tristram Shandy, so he is a writer.

clue.text: Robert Graves's children possessed it

parts.note: a quality held by children in a Robert Graves poem: insight beyond their years

explanation.definitionFit: The quality children have in Graves's poem is sound judgement and insight.

clue.text: "The Courts where Jamshyd gloried and deep" (Fitzgerald)

definitions.text: "The Courts where Jamshyd gloried and deep" (Fitzgerald)

parts.words: "The Courts where Jamshyd gloried and deep" (Fitzgerald)
parts.note: a gap-fill from FitzGerald's Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam: the missing word follows 'and' and goes with 'deep'

explanation.surface: A line of FitzGerald's Rubaiyat with a word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: FitzGerald's line has Jamshyd gloried and then imbibed deep, the past tense of the verb meaning took a drink.

clue.text: Poem concerning which Larkin saved the clip pings?

definitions.text: Poem concerning which Larkin saved the clip pings

parts.words: Poem concerning which Larkin saved the clip pings
parts.note: Philip Larkin wrote a poem about mown lawn; the clippings are the mown blades, not press cuttings

explanation.surface: Larkin kept newspaper cuttings about one of his poems.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clippings' suggests press cuttings, but it means what a mower leaves on the lawn, the subject of Larkin's poem of 1971.
explanation.definitionFit: Larkin's short poem about mown meadow blades carries this two-word title.

clue.text: A friend of Nicholas (in short, it's Michael) Entries submitted from

parts.note: it's shortened is just 's, as 'in short' says
Mike is the short form of Michael

explanation.surface: Nicholas's friend is called Michael for short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in short' tells you to shorten both words: it's to S and Michael to MIKE. Smike is Nicholas Nickleby's loyal friend in Dickens.
explanation.definitionFit: Smike is the poor boy rescued from Dotheboys Hall who becomes Nicholas Nickleby's devoted companion.

clue.text: Official proceedings in tract (arrant nonsense, of course)

indicators.note: in says the answer sits inside the words that follow, spanning the bracket

explanation.surface: Records of a body set out in a pamphlet, which the clue calls rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'tract (arrant'; the bracketed 'arrant nonsense, of course' is the setter's aside, a link with no letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for 'things done', it names the formal minutes or records of a society.

clue.text: Plain tale from Cooper

definitions.meaning: a wide treeless grassland
James Fenimore Cooper's novel The Prairie (1827)

explanation.definitionFit: A wide grassland of North America gives Fenimore Cooper's frontier novel its title.

clue.text: Undercover operator is both English poet and French marshal

explanation.surface: A secret agent is at once a poet and a soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Percy Blakeney is the Scarlet Pimpernel, who rescues aristocrats in disguise in Baroness Orczy's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Percy, the Scarlet Pimpernel, works in disguise to rescue victims of the Terror.

definitions.text: "When last I was at —— The mayor in courtesy show'd me the castle" (Richard III)

parts.words: "When last I was at —— The mayor in courtesy show'd me the castle" (Richard III)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Shakespeare's Richard III: the king names the Devon city whose castle is Rougemont

explanation.surface: A line of Shakespeare's Richard III with a place name missing.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Richard III the king recalls the mayor of this Devon cathedral city showing him Rougemont Castle.
